scenes.kicker: Claude API tutorial · step by step
scenes.title:
Claude Tools & the Tool Runner
[[The Tool Use Lifecycle]]
scenes.subtitle: Give Claude your own functions, and understand every stop_reason

lines.say: Claude is great with words. But on its own, it can't check your database, call your API, or look up a customer's order.
Tools fix that. In this video, you'll learn how tools work, the full tool use lifecycle with stop reasons, and how the Tool Runner handles the loop for you.
We'll build a real example, step by step, in Python.

scenes.heading: What is a [[tool]]?
items: A function you **describe** to Claude: a name, a description, an input schema
Claude **decides** when to call it, and with which inputs
Claude **never runs it**: your code does, then sends back the result

lines.say: So, what is a tool?
A tool is a function you describe to Claude, with three parts: a name, a description, and an input schema, which is a JSON schema for its parameters.
Claude reads that description, and decides when to call the tool, and with which inputs.
But here's the key idea: Claude never runs anything itself. It asks. Your code runs the function, and sends the result back.
Some tools, like web search, run on Anthropic's servers instead. Today: your own tools.

rows.label: You run it and send a tool_result

lines.say: Here's the tool use lifecycle. Every tool call is a round trip.
One: you send the conversation, plus your list of tools.
Two: if Claude wants a tool, the response comes back with stop reason, tool use. It contains a tool use block, with an id, the tool name, and the input.
lines.tts: Two: if Claude wants a tool, the response comes back with stop reason: tool use. It contains a tool use block, with an I D, the tool name, and the input.

lines.say: Three: you run the tool, and send back a tool result, with the same id. Then Claude writes its answer, with stop reason, end turn.
lines.tts: Three: you run the tool, and send back a tool result, with the same I D. Then Claude writes its answer, with stop reason: end turn.

lines.say: Claude may call tools several times in a row. So the rule is simple: keep looping while the stop reason is tool use.
Let's look closer. On the left, Claude's request: the tool name, the input it chose, and a unique id.
lines.tts: Let's look closer. On the left, Claude's request: the tool name, the input it chose, and a unique I D.

lines.say: On the right, your answer, sent as a user message. The tool use id links the result to the request. And is error tells Claude if the tool failed.
lines.tts: On the right, your answer, sent as a user message. The tool use I D links the result to the request. And is error tells Claude if the tool failed.

lines.say: Two rules: the tool result must come right after Claude's tool use message, and tool results go first in the message content.

left.title: Use a tool when you need…
left.body:
• Actions: send, write, update
• Fresh or private data:
  prices, orders, your database
• A guaranteed JSON shape
• Your existing APIs and systems

right.title: Skip tools when…
right.body:
• Claude can answer alone:
  summaries, translation
• It's one-shot Q&A with
  nothing to execute
• The extra round trip costs
  more than the task

lines.say: When should you use a tool?
When Claude needs to do something, like send or update. When it needs fresh or private data, like your orders. Or when you need a guaranteed JSON shape.
Skip tools when Claude can answer from text alone, like a summary or a translation. Every tool call is an extra round trip.

left.title: Without a tool
left.body:
Customer: "Where is order 1042?"

Claude can't see your orders.
It can only apologize,
or worse, guess.

right.title: With get_order_status
right.body:
Claude calls the tool
→ your code reads orders.json
→ "Order 1042 has shipped
   with DHL, arriving Oct 23"

✓ Real data, every time

lines.say: Our use case: an order status assistant for a small online shop.
Without a tool, Claude can't see the orders. It can only apologize.
With a get order status tool, Claude asks for the data, our code reads it, and the answer is based on real data.
Here's the project: the orders in a JSON file, and a small function that looks one up.

do.text:
import json
import pathlib

HERE = pathlib.Path(__file__).parent
ORDERS = json.loads((HERE / "orders.json").read_text())


def get_order_status(order_id: str) -> str:
    """Return the order as JSON, or raise a helpful error."""
    order = ORDERS.get(order_id)
    if order is None:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Order {order_id} not found. Ask the customer to "
            "check the number in their confirmation email.")
    return json.dumps(order)

lines.say: If the order doesn't exist, it raises an error with a clear message. We'll come back to that.
First, I ask Claude about an order, with no tools at all.

do.text:
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user",
               "content": "Where is my order 1042?"}],
)
print("stop_reason:", response.stop_reason)
print(response.content[0].text)

out: I don't have access to your order information.

lines.say: Stop reason: end turn. Claude finished, but it simply can't know. Let's give it a tool.
Step one: define the tool.
I import the SDK and my function, then describe the tool in a list: a name, a description, and an input schema.
The description matters most. Claude reads it to decide when to call the tool. The docs recommend three or four sentences: what it does, and when to use it.
The input schema says the tool takes one required string: the order id.
lines.tts: The input schema says the tool takes one required string: the order I D.

lines.say: Step two: run the lifecycle loop.
Inside a while loop, I call the API with the tools, and print the stop reason. If it's not tool use, Claude is done, so I break.

do.text:
while True:
    response = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=1024,
        tools=tools, messages=messages,
    )
    print("stop_reason:", response.stop_reason)
    if response.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break
    messages.append({"role": "assistant",
                     "content": response.content})
    results = []
    for block in response.content:
        if block.type == "tool_use":
            print(f"  tool call: {block.name}({block.input})")
            output = get_order_status(**block.input)
            results.append({"type": "tool_result",
                            "tool_use_id": block.id,
                            "content": output})
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})

print("".join(b.text for b in response.content
              if b.type == "text"))

lines.say: Otherwise, I append Claude's message, run each tool use block, and send back a tool result with the same id. Then the loop calls Claude again.
lines.tts: Otherwise, I append Claude's message, run each tool use block, and send back a tool result with the same I D. Then the loop calls Claude again.

lines.say: Now, let's run it, and watch the stop reasons.

out: Your order 1042 has shipped with DHL and should

lines.say: There's the lifecycle: first tool use, my code runs the function, then end turn, with an answer based on real data. Claude's wording will differ in your run.
Step three: the Tool Runner. That loop works, but you'd write it in every project. The SDK can do it for you.
With the beta tool decorator, my plain Python function becomes a tool. The SDK builds the schema from the type hints and the docstring.

do.text:
import anthropic
from anthropic import beta_tool
import shop_tools

client = anthropic.Anthropic()


@beta_tool
def get_order_status(order_id: str) -> str:
    """Look up a my-shop order by its number.

    Returns the status, carrier and delivery date.
    Use it whenever a customer asks where their order is.

    Args:
        order_id: Order number, e.g. 1042
    """
    return shop_tools.get_order_status(order_id)

lines.say: Then the tool runner, which is in beta in the official SDKs. It runs the tools, appends the messages, and loops until Claude stops calling tools.

do.text:
runner = client.beta.messages.tool_runner(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    max_iterations=5,
    tools=[get_order_status],
    messages=[
        {"role": "user",
         "content": "Where are my orders 1042 and 9999?"},
    ],
)
for message in runner:
    print("stop_reason:", message.stop_reason)

print("".join(b.text for b in message.content
              if b.type == "text"))

lines.say: Max iterations puts a safety limit on the loop. And I still get each message, to print its stop reason.
Step four: handle errors. This time, I ask about two orders: ten forty-two, and nine thousand nine hundred ninety-nine, which doesn't exist.
Claude calls the tool twice, in one turn. For nine nine nine nine, my function raises an error.

out: Error occurred while calling tool: get_order_status
ValueError: Order 9999 not found. Ask the customer to
check the number in their confirmation email.
Order 1042 has shipped with DHL and should arrive on
October 23. I couldn't find order 9999: could you check
the number in your confirmation email?

lines.say: The Tool Runner catches it, and sends it to Claude as a tool result with is error set to true. The script doesn't crash.
And because my error message says what to do next, Claude answers the first order, and asks the customer to check the second number.
In the manual loop, you'd catch the exception yourself, and set is error in the tool result.

lines.say: Step five: know every stop reason, because your code should check it on every response.
End turn: Claude finished. Use the answer.
Tool use: run the tool, and send the result back.
Max tokens: the answer hit your max tokens limit, so it's cut off. Raise the limit, or continue the response.
Stop sequence: Claude wrote one of your custom stop sequences.
Pause turn: a server tool, like web search, hit its loop limit. Send the conversation back, and Claude continues.
Refusal: Claude declined to respond. Check the stop details. There's also model context window exceeded, when the response fills the context window.

cards.title: Describe in detail
cards.text: What it does, when to use it, each parameter

cards.title: Write helpful errors
cards.text: Say what went wrong and what to try next

cards.title: Always bound the loop
cards.text: `max_iterations`, or a counter in your loop

cards.title: Need approval? Go manual
cards.text: Manual loop for human-in-the-loop and logging

lines.say: Four tips before you ship.
One: write detailed descriptions. It's the biggest factor in how well Claude uses your tools.
Two: write helpful error messages. Say what went wrong, and what to try next, so Claude can recover.
Three: always bound the loop, with max iterations, or a counter in your own loop.
And four: the Tool Runner is the easy default. When you need human approval before a tool runs, custom logging, or conditional execution, use the manual loop.

scenes.heading: Recap
items: A tool = name + description + input schema; **your code** runs it
Loop while `stop_reason` is `tool_use`; send back a `tool_result`
The [[Tool Runner]] runs the loop and turns errors into `is_error`

lines.say: Let's recap.
A tool is a name, a description, and an input schema. Claude asks, and your code runs it.
The lifecycle: loop while the stop reason is tool use, and send back a tool result with the same id.
lines.tts: The lifecycle: loop while the stop reason is tool use, and send back a tool result with the same I D.

lines.say: And the Tool Runner runs that loop for you, and turns your exceptions into is error results.
